title: Optimal Operation of Battery Swapping Stations for Electric Vehicles with Grid Energy Services: A Battery Resource Allocation Approach
content: A battery swapping station (BSS) exchanges a depleted electric-vehicle pack for a charged one in minutes, and its shelf of batteries doubles as a grid-connected store that can buy energy when it is cheap and sell it back when it is dear. Running the two businesses together is a scheduling problem: when to charge each pack, when to discharge to the grid, and which pack to hand to which customer. This paper sets that problem out as battery resource allocation (BatRes). In its general form the model is a mixed-integer program, because the request-to-battery assignment is binary and a no-simultaneous-charge-and-discharge condition is nonlinear. Under a first-come-first-served rule the assignment is fixed, and because conversion losses are charged on both power directions the nonlinear condition never binds at the optimum; the model that is actually solved is therefore a linear program, solved to global optimality. Two cases are reported under the industrial time-of-use tariff of Pakistan: a small three-request, two-battery, twelve-slot case that can be read decision by decision, and a reproducible synthetic full-day case with thirty requests across eight batteries. In the small case, net profit ranges from PKR 939.2 to PKR 994.7 across the six arrival orders, and adding the swap business raises profit to about four times the grid-energy-services-only level at this tariff and swap price. Sensitivity sweeps over the swap price, tariff premium, inventory size, efficiency, and depth of discharge map how each shifts the result. Every figure is specific to the assumed tariff, service price, deterministic demand, and station parameters, and is presented as such.
